title: 3-Digit Addition and Subtraction Worksheets Within 1,000
intro: Use hundreds, tens, and ones to make larger calculations understandable. This mixed set keeps quantities and answers within 1,000 and leaves space for a drawing, a split-number strategy, or a written calculation.
html:
A larger number still has parts you can work with

Jordan sees 368 + 257 and worries that the numbers are too large to hold in mind. Instead of treating each number as one difficult block, separate the second number into two hundreds, five tens, and seven ones. Each part can be added in a manageable step.

368 + 200 = 568
568 + 50 = 618
618 + 7 = 625

All three steps together add 257, so 368 + 257 = 625.

Understand the exchanges in a written method

A written addition method reaches the same result by combining equal place values. Eight ones plus seven ones make fifteen ones: one ten and five ones. Six tens plus five tens plus the exchanged ten make twelve tens: one hundred and two tens. Three hundreds plus two hundreds plus the exchanged hundred make six hundreds.

The result is six hundreds, two tens, and five ones. Naming the units helps a child understand why a small written 1 can represent ten in one column and one hundred in another. Its position gives it its value.

Use the same structure for subtraction

For 602 − 278, a child cannot remove eight ones from two ones without regrouping. There are no tens available, so first exchange one hundred for ten tens. Then exchange one of those tens for ten ones. Six hundred two becomes five hundreds, nine tens, and twelve ones; its total value stays 602.

602 = 500 + 90 + 12
602 − 278 = 324
324 + 278 = 602

If the child loses a ten while crossing a zero: draw the hundreds, tens, and ones after each exchange. Check that the drawing still represents 602 before subtracting. Regrouping changes the form of the number, not its amount.

Choose a strategy and check the result

Some questions are easier with mental steps. Subtracting 199, for example, can be done by subtracting 200 and adding one back. Other questions may suit a written method. Ask the child to explain one choice rather than requiring the same method on every line.

These twelve horizontal questions allow room for working. The set can include zero and one-, two-, or three-digit numbers, and a quantity can reach 1,000. “Within 1,000” is an upper limit; this is not a set in which every number has exactly three digits. Use addition to check subtraction and compare the result with a rough estimate.
